books.section: Topic 4.10 The Second Great Awakening, A. Religious and Spiritual Movements in Antebellum America
Topic 4.10 The Second Great Awakening, Transcendentalism

primary_sources: Charles G. Finney, "What a Revival of Religion Is," 1835
Margaret Fuller, Woman in the Nineteenth Century, 1845
Henry David Thoreau, Walden; or, Life in the Woods (1854)

source: original; documents are public-domain primary sources or paraphrases of them (see each document's sourcing note)
prompt: Evaluate the extent to which the Second Great Awakening transformed American religion and society in the period 1800-1860.

documents.title: Cane Ridge camp meeting
documents.source: Paraphrase of the Disciples of Christ Historical Society account of the Cane Ridge Revival, August 1801. Public domain.
documents.sourcing: A Presbyterian minister's meeting draws a crowd no church could hold.
documents.text: In August 1801, Barton W. Stone hosted a communion service at Cane Ridge, Kentucky, that drew ten to twenty thousand people for six days, though the log meetinghouse seated only about four hundred. Presbyterian, Methodist, and Baptist preachers all preached, and hundreds took communion at tables set up in the woods.

documents.title: A new church in the burned-over district
documents.source: Paraphrase of Barron's Premium 2027, Chapter 6, Topic 4.10, Mormonism. Public domain.
documents.sourcing: A new sect grows in the revival country of upstate New York.
documents.text: In 1830, Joseph Smith published the Book of Mormon in Palmyra, New York, and founded the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints. The church grew in the religious ferment of upstate New York, then moved as a community from New York to Ohio, Missouri, and Illinois.

documents.title: Finney on revival
documents.source: Charles G. Finney, "What a Revival of Religion Is," Lectures on Revivals of Religion, 1835. Public domain.
documents.sourcing: A famous revivalist promises that even the worst sinners can be converted.
documents.text: "When the churches are thus awakened and reformed, the reformation and salvation of sinners will follow.... Their hearts will be broken down and changed. Very often the most abandoned profligates are among the subjects. Harlots, and drunkards, and infidels, and all sorts of abandoned characters, are awakened and converted."

documents.title: Emerson's American Scholar
documents.source: Ralph Waldo Emerson, "The American Scholar," address at Cambridge, Massachusetts, August 31, 1837. Public domain.
documents.sourcing: A lecturer tells Harvard's Phi Beta Kappa Society that American learning must stand on its own.
documents.text: "Our day of dependence, our long apprenticeship to the learning of other lands, draws to a close. The millions that around us are rushing into life cannot always be fed on the sere remains of foreign harvests. Events, actions arise, that must be sung, that will sing themselves."

documents.title: Emerson on self-reliance
documents.source: Ralph Waldo Emerson, "Self-Reliance," Essays: First Series, 1841. Public domain.
documents.sourcing: An essayist tells readers to trust their own judgment over custom and conformity.
documents.text: "Trust thyself: every heart vibrates to that iron string. Accept the place the divine providence has found for you, the society of your contemporaries, the connection of events."

documents.title: Fuller on women
documents.source: Paraphrase of Margaret Fuller, Woman in the Nineteenth Century, 1845. Public domain.
documents.sourcing: A writer in Emerson's circle extends the idea of self-trust to women.
documents.text: Fuller argued that women, like men, should be free to develop their minds and characters. She wrote as a member of the transcendentalist circle in Concord, and her book fed the generation that met for women's rights at Seneca Falls in 1848.

documents.title: Thoreau at Walden Pond
documents.source: Henry David Thoreau, Walden; or, Life in the Woods, 1854. Public domain.
documents.sourcing: A writer explains why he left ordinary life for two years in a cabin by a pond.
documents.text: "I went to the woods because I wished to live deliberately, to front only the essential facts of life, and see if I could not learn what it had to teach, and not, when I came to die, discover that I had not lived."

rubric.criterion: Thesis: earns the point for a historically defensible claim that answers the prompt, stating the extent to which the Second Great Awakening transformed American religion and society, with a clear line of reasoning.
rubric.notEarned: Restating the prompt with no claim about the extent of change does not earn the point.

rubric.criterion: Contextualization: earns the point for describing a broader historical context relevant to the prompt, such as the market revolution, the expansion of white male democracy, or the growth of reform movements.
rubric.notEarned: A sentence of background with no link to the argument does not earn the point.

rubric.criterion: Evidence from documents (first point): earns the point for describing the content of at least three documents relevant to the argument.
rubric.notEarned: Quoting documents without describing what they show does not earn the point.

rubric.criterion: Evidence from documents (second point): earns the point for using the content of at least six documents to support the argument.
rubric.notEarned: Using fewer than six documents, or using six without tying them to the argument, does not earn the point.

rubric.criterion: Evidence beyond the documents: earns the point for describing a specific relevant example not in the documents, such as the burned-over district, Brook Farm, the Oneida Community, Handsome Lake's Longhouse Religion, or temperance and abolition.
rubric.notEarned: A vague reference to outside knowledge with no specific example does not earn the point.

rubric.criterion: Sourcing: earns the point for explaining how the audience, purpose, historical situation, or point of view of at least two documents shapes the argument.
rubric.notEarned: Naming a document's author without explaining how it shapes the argument does not earn the point.

rubric.criterion: Complexity: earns the point for a complex argument, such as qualifying the thesis by showing where the Awakening transformed religion and society and where its reach stopped, or who it included and left out.
rubric.notEarned: A second example with no qualification or weighing does not earn the point.

modelOutline:
Thesis: The Second Great Awakening transformed American religion and society to a great extent between 1800 and 1860, remaking how Americans worshipped and giving reform movements their moral engine, yet its transformation was uneven, reaching some Americans deeply and passing others by.
Context: The market revolution was pulling farmers, merchants, and workers into a cash economy, white men were voting in numbers the founders never imagined, and Americans were asking what their democracy meant.
Grouping: Documents 1, 2, and 3 show the revival itself: Cane Ridge crowds no church could hold, a new Mormon church born in the burned-over district, and Finney's promise that any sinner could choose conversion. Documents 4, 5, and 7 show the idea turning inward: Emerson's call for intellectual independence, his doctrine of self-trust, and Thoreau's deliberate life at Walden Pond. Document 6 extends it: Fuller carries self-trust to women.
Beyond the documents: Brook Farm and the Oneida Community tried communal life, Handsome Lake built a Native teaching from Seneca tradition and Quaker ideas, and revival energy fed temperance and abolition.
Complexity: The transformation was real but bounded: transcendentalism stayed a small Concord circle, the Mormons answered hostility by leaving American society rather than reforming it, and enslaved people and immigrants stood largely outside the revival's churches.
